transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE); Mason Chu (Redwood SE); Priya Nair (Orion SRE); Daniel Kim (Orion Platform); Ruth Alvarez (Orion Security)

Summary: quick follow up from the outage on Nov 10 where we saw a cascading latency spike when a heavy batched job hit the hosted runtime and fell back to a slower model variant; this is the 30min follow-up to validate the patch and next steps.

Topics: patch status, rollout plan, KV cache behavior, autoscaling thresholds, security doc follow-ups, pricing for Dedicated burst.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: okay everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is the postmortem follow up for the 11/10 incident. we wanted to go over the patched runtime and make sure the rollback and the mitigation plan are clear. mason do you want to start with the changes?
[00:26] Mason Chu: yeah sure, uh hi all. quick recap: root cause was a combination of prefix KV cache thrashing and a fallback path that switched to a high-latency quantized model under some memory pressure conditions. we pushed a patch that changes the kv-cache eviction policy and tightens the fallback threshold so requests don't move to the slower variant unless absolutely necessary.
[00:50] Priya Nair: when you say "kv-cache" are you talking about the prefix cache at the runtime level or the cache in our gateway? cause we saw a bunch of cache misses that looked like they were coming from your side.
[01:05] Mason Chu: good question. it's the runtime prefix cache — the one that lives on the GPU host; sometimes transcribed as K-V cash in the logs, i know, but it's the GPU-resident cache. we saw a scenario where concurrent long-running sessions caused rapid eviction which then triggered the fallback.
[01:30] Daniel Kim: and that eviction was correlated with the burst, right? like when we had the analytics job, traffic was non-uniform, microbursts.
[01:38] Mason Chu: exactly, high skew. the compactor was too eager under that pattern. the patch reduces eviction aggressiveness and adds a short warm-up window so newly loaded kv entries aren't evicted immediately.
[01:53] Ruth Alvarez: from security perspective, i want to confirm the patch doesn't change encryption behavior or KMS calls — we saw some alerts during the incident about increased upstream calls.
[02:05] Mason Chu: it doesn't touch KMS or encryption; those alerts were a side-effect of retry storming from the gateway. patch removes some of the retry amplification by bounding internal request fan-out.
[02:20] Priya Nair: okay good. can you describe the rollout plan? are you planning a canary to our Dedicated pool or to hosted first?
[02:30] Lena Ortiz: our recommendation is to stage it on your staging Dedicated pool first — that gives you the same resource isolation and lets you run 2x load tests. after you validate, we can promote to production with a canary route (5% traffic for 30 mins).
[02:47] Daniel Kim: timeline on the binary?
[02:50] Mason Chu: we'll push the patched build and a perf regression report by tomorrow, 2027-11-16; note there is a slight memory tradeoff — retention of more KV entries means peak GPU memory up by roughly 40-60MB per model shard, we measured that in our benchmarks.
[03:10] Priya Nair: that memory bump could matter for us because our Dedicated pool is tight. what's the suggestion if we can't add more memory?
[03:18] Mason Chu: two options: enable the new eviction policy with an explicit limit and a slightly higher fallback threshold, or temporarily increase Dedicated burst capacity while we tune. the former reduces the memory increase but keeps most latency benefits.
[03:31] Lena Ortiz: also note that if you prefer Hosted, we can route high-volume jobs to a higher-tier capacity automatically, but that has cost implications. we'll send updated pricing for the burst option.
[03:45] Ruth Alvarez: on compliance items, we still need the SOC2 excerpts and the KMS integration docs for our review. i filed a request last week.
[03:55] Lena Ortiz: i have that as an action item — i'll get you the relevant snippets by 11/17. mason, you ok to pull the SOC2 section?
[04:04] Mason Chu: yep i'll pull the SOC2/ISO excerpts and also a short note on audit logs retention; i think robo logs weren't collected during the incident because of a rotation mismatch, we'll include fix notes.
[04:20] Priya Nair: quick note — during the incident we saw fallbacks to the quantized model which changed result distributions a little; that was flagged by our QA. will the patch prevent that or do we need a separate rollout of a model variant?
[04:35] Mason Chu: the patch reduces the conditions that trigger the fallback; it doesn't change the quantized model itself. if you want to avoid any potential distribution shift we'll hold canary traffic at 0% and first validate with synthetic workloads that compare outputs.
[04:50] Daniel Kim: can we also get a short guide on how to pin model versions in your routing layer? our platform team would like deterministic behavior during biz-critical runs.
[04:59] Lena Ortiz: absolutely — we'll send configuration docs for pinning model versions and for creating route policies (latency vs cost vs region).
[05:10] Priya Nair: earlier you mentioned retry amplification — any immediate mitigation we should apply on our gateway side?
[05:17] Mason Chu: yes, throttling on the gateway with an exponential backoff cap reduces amplification; also limiting concurrent in-flight requests per session helps. we'll include recommended settings in the notes.
[05:32] Ruth Alvarez: on audit logs, can you confirm retention windows and whether logs include token-level correlation? we need that for our audit.
[05:41] Mason Chu: audit logs include token-level latency and per-request model info, they are stored in the control plane for 90 days by default; we can extend retention for enterprise plans. we'll confirm exact fields in the doc.
[05:56] Priya Nair: sounds good. next, can we talk about regression testing? we want to make sure the patch doesn't regress throughput on our longer sequences.
[06:06] Mason Chu: we ran a battery of tests; with the new policy throughput for long-seq workloads is within 3% of baseline in our env, and latency improved for short sequences. we'll attach the perf spreadsheet.
[06:20] Daniel Kim: please include the exact test harness commands — otherwise reproducing results is tricky.
[06:26] Mason Chu: yep will do. also note there is a nondeterministic path in the cache compactor where under extreme memory pressure it still might evict more aggressively; we're working on a follow-up change to make that deterministic.
[06:42] Priya Nair: is that follow-up a code change that could be backported quickly or will it be a longer effort?
[06:48] Mason Chu: medium-term, maybe 2 sprints; but the current patch reduces the odds significantly. if you need something faster we can enable a config flag to disable compaction entirely for a short window — that increases memory usage but makes eviction behavior predictable.
[07:05] Lena Ortiz: for clarity, we'll provide three remediation tracks in the notes: immediate (gateway throttles + config flag), near-term (patch we just discussed), and medium-term (compactor rewrite).
[07:18] Ruth Alvarez: thanks. regarding encryption, if we increase Dedicated burst or change routing, does that change key residency or HSM access patterns?
[07:29] Mason Chu: no change to KMS/HSM residency — keys remain in your tenant's KMS if using Dedicated. for Hosted we handle envelope encryption but never access plaintext. we'll add a diagram to the security appendix.
[07:45] Priya Nair: any customer-facing messages? we had internal alerts — do you want us to share a joint status note or do you want Redwood to publish?
[07:55] Lena Ortiz: let's draft a joint postmortem summary; Redwood will provide a template and you can insert internal specifics. we'll also include mitigations and timeline.
[08:06] Daniel Kim: last question — competitors. we looked at OtherCloudAI's managed endpoint earlier; they do auto-scaling differently. did you see anything in the patch that would affect comparables?
[08:18] Mason Chu: only in the sense that our new eviction policy trades a small memory increase for lower tail latency; some vendors opt for stateless scaling which avoids KV cache complexity but increases cost per token. we'll include a short note in the notes.
[08:35] Lena Ortiz: ok let's recap action items — mason to send binary and perf report by 11/16, lena to send pricing and SOC2 snippets by 11/17, priya to run staging load test by 11/19, ruth to confirm KMS constraints by 11/17.
[08:54] Priya Nair: yep thanks all. one last thing — can we schedule the KV cache deep-dive for next week?
[08:59] Mason Chu: i'll propose times after this call.
[09:02] Lena Ortiz: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with the artifacts and link to the staging runbook.

End of transcript.
